title: OPPI Data Hub Redesign
strategicSummary: Redesigned a complex government data hub to improve accessibility, usability, and navigation clarity for diverse public audiences.
responsibilities: Led discovery workshops with stakeholders
Conducted IA audit of existing site structure
Developed new site map and navigation taxonomy
Created user flows for primary task scenarios
Documented requirements and acceptance criteria
Facilitated usability review sessions
overview: The OPPI Data Hub serves as a central resource for public-sector data across multiple agencies. The existing site had grown organically over several years, resulting in fragmented navigation, inconsistent taxonomy, and barriers for users with disabilities. This project focused on restructuring the information architecture to create a clear, accessible, and intuitive experience.
problemAndGoals: The primary challenge was a disorganized content structure that made it difficult for users to locate relevant datasets and reports. Business goals included reducing support requests by 30%, improving time-on-task for data retrieval, and achieving WCAG 2.1 AA compliance. Stakeholders needed a scalable architecture that could accommodate future content growth without requiring a full redesign.
myRole: As UX Strategist and Information Architect, I owned the discovery process from stakeholder interviews through final IA documentation. I collaborated closely with the development team to ensure the proposed architecture was technically feasible and with the content team to align taxonomy with existing workflows.
discoveryAndConstraints: Discovery included 12 stakeholder interviews, competitive analysis of 5 comparable data portals, and review of existing analytics to understand top user tasks. Key constraints included a fixed CMS platform, a tight 6-month timeline, and the need to preserve all existing URLs for SEO continuity.
informationArchitecture: The new IA reduced the top-level navigation from 9 items to 5, introduced a consistent tagging taxonomy for datasets, and established a clear hierarchy distinguishing raw data from interpretive reports. A new search-first pattern was implemented for power users alongside a browse-by-category path for casual visitors.
userFlows: Three primary user flows were designed: finding and downloading a specific dataset, exploring available data by agency, and accessing the latest published reports. Each flow was mapped from entry point through task completion, with decision nodes documented for edge cases and error states.
wireframesAndPrototypes: Mid-fidelity wireframes were created in Figma for all primary templates: homepage, category landing, dataset detail, and search results. An interactive prototype was used in three rounds of stakeholder review, with each round producing documented feedback and a revised iteration.
requirementsAndCriteria: Requirements were documented in Confluence, organized by user story. Each requirement included acceptance criteria written in Given/When/Then format. Accessibility requirements were integrated throughout rather than treated as a separate checklist, covering keyboard navigation, screen reader compatibility, and color contrast.
qaAndIteration: QA included a structured content audit against the new taxonomy, heuristic evaluation of the prototype, and accessibility testing with both automated tools and manual screen reader review. Three iteration cycles addressed navigation labeling, filter behavior, and mobile layout issues identified during review.
outcomesAndNextSteps: The redesigned architecture was approved by all stakeholder groups and handed off to development with complete documentation. Early usability testing showed a 40% reduction in time-on-task for the primary data retrieval scenario. Next steps include a post-launch content audit at 90 days and ongoing analytics review to validate the taxonomy assumptions.

title: Pikes Peak Library District Website Redesign
strategicSummary: Led IA and content strategy for a large public library system website, unifying 12 branch locations under a coherent, accessible digital experience.
responsibilities: Facilitated community discovery sessions
Audited 800+ pages of existing content
Designed unified navigation architecture
Developed content templates and standards
Created accessibility requirements documentation
Coordinated with branch librarians on local content needs
overview: Pikes Peak Library District operates 12 branch locations and serves a diverse community across El Paso County, Colorado. Their website had grown into a fragmented collection of microsites with inconsistent navigation, outdated content structures, and significant accessibility barriers. This project unified the digital presence under a single, coherent information architecture.
problemAndGoals: Users struggled to find branch hours, event registrations, and digital resource access across a site with three competing navigation systems. The goal was to create one unified IA that served both casual visitors and frequent library users, reduced content maintenance burden for staff, and met WCAG 2.1 AA standards.
myRole: I led the IA and content strategy workstreams, coordinating with the district's communications team, branch managers, and an external design agency. My deliverables included the content audit, new site map, content templates, and the accessibility requirements specification.
discoveryAndConstraints: Discovery included community listening sessions at three branch locations, surveys distributed to library card holders, and interviews with 8 branch staff members responsible for web content. The primary constraint was a new CMS that had already been procured, requiring the IA to work within its templating system.
informationArchitecture: The new site map consolidated from 4 navigation structures to 1, with clear separation between 'Visit' (physical locations and hours), 'Borrow' (catalog and digital resources), 'Learn' (programs and events), and 'About' (district information). Branch pages were standardized using a single template with locally editable zones.
userFlows: Key flows designed included: finding a branch and its hours, registering for a library card, discovering and registering for events, and accessing digital resources remotely. Each flow accounted for both logged-in and anonymous user states.
wireframesAndPrototypes: Wireframes covered 14 distinct page templates, from the homepage through event detail and digital resource landing pages. Prototypes were tested with 8 community members representing different digital literacy levels and accessibility needs.
requirementsAndCriteria: Content requirements specified writing standards, reading level targets (Grade 8 or below for public-facing content), image alt text standards, and structured data requirements for events. Technical requirements covered search indexing, language support, and emergency alert display.
qaAndIteration: Content audit was conducted against the new taxonomy to identify gaps, duplicates, and pages requiring rewrite before migration. Accessibility QA included automated scanning of all wireframes and manual review of interactive components for keyboard and screen reader compatibility.
outcomesAndNextSteps: The new architecture reduced top-level navigation items by 55% and standardized 800+ pages into 14 reusable templates. Staff feedback indicated a significant reduction in time required for routine content updates. Post-launch plans include a 6-month content review cycle and accessibility audit.

title: Colorado Springs Utilities Public Information Flyer
strategicSummary: Redesigned public utility communications to improve content clarity, plain language compliance, and accessibility for a diverse municipal audience.
responsibilities: Audited existing communications for clarity and accessibility
Applied plain language principles to technical content
Developed content hierarchy and layout recommendations
Created accessible design specifications
Reviewed translated materials for Spanish-speaking audiences
overview: Colorado Springs Utilities distributes public information materials to hundreds of thousands of customers across the Pikes Peak region. Many of these materials used technical language, dense formatting, and layouts that created barriers for residents with varying literacy levels or visual disabilities. This project applied content strategy and plain language principles to improve communication effectiveness.
problemAndGoals: Customer service data showed high call volumes related to information already present in distributed materials, indicating comprehension failures rather than information gaps. Goals included improving first-read comprehension, reducing calls related to billing and service information, and ensuring materials met Section 508 accessibility requirements.
myRole: As Content Strategist, I audited the existing materials library, identified content patterns causing confusion, and developed rewrite and redesign recommendations. I also created a content style guide specific to utility communications and reviewed Spanish-language versions for translation quality.
discoveryAndConstraints: Discovery included review of customer service call logs to identify common confusion points, readability analysis of 24 existing documents, and interviews with frontline customer service staff. Constraints included brand guidelines that required significant negotiation to update, and printing specifications that limited layout flexibility.
informationArchitecture: Documents were restructured using a consistent hierarchy: key action or message first, supporting detail second, and reference information last. Recurring content blocks were identified and standardized across the materials library to reduce inconsistency.
userFlows: Customer journeys were mapped for the three highest-call-volume scenarios: understanding a higher-than-expected bill, setting up automatic payment, and reporting a service issue. Each journey identified the touchpoints where written materials played a role and where content gaps created friction.
wireframesAndPrototypes: Layout prototypes were developed for 6 high-priority document types, demonstrating improved visual hierarchy, white space, and typography. Each prototype included annotations explaining the content strategy rationale for key decisions.
requirementsAndCriteria: A content requirements document specified reading level targets (Grade 6-8), required accessibility metadata for digital versions, approved terminology for technical concepts, and review process requirements for future updates.
qaAndIteration: Materials were reviewed by customer service staff for accuracy, tested for readability using automated tools, and reviewed against Section 508 requirements. Two iteration cycles addressed terminology concerns from technical reviewers and layout adjustments for print production.
outcomesAndNextSteps: Revised materials showed an average reading level reduction of 2.3 grade levels and improved Section 508 compliance scores. The content style guide was adopted by the communications team for ongoing use. Next steps include extending the approach to digital communications and developing templates for routine notices.

title: Peak Vista Digital Style & Content Guide
strategicSummary: Created a comprehensive digital style and content guide to standardize web communications across a multi-location community health organization.
responsibilities: Audited existing digital content for consistency issues
Conducted stakeholder interviews across departments
Developed voice, tone, and style guidelines
Created component-level content standards
Facilitated training sessions for content contributors
Maintained guide in Confluence with version control
overview: Peak Vista Community Health Centers operates multiple locations serving underserved populations across southern Colorado. Their digital presence had grown without consistent standards, resulting in inconsistent voice, variable content quality, and patient-facing information that varied significantly across location pages. This project established a comprehensive digital style and content guide to unify their communications.
problemAndGoals: Different departments and locations were publishing web content independently, resulting in brand inconsistency, conflicting information, and accessibility gaps. The goal was to create a practical, usable guide that non-specialist content contributors could apply without deep UX knowledge, while ensuring all content met accessibility and plain language standards.
myRole: As the Documentation Lead, I owned the guide from initial audit through final publication and training. I collaborated with the marketing director, clinical communications team, and IT department to ensure the guide addressed real workflows and integrated with existing CMS capabilities.
discoveryAndConstraints: Discovery included a content audit of 200+ web pages, interviews with 10 content contributors across departments, and analysis of patient feedback related to digital communications. A key constraint was that the guide needed to be maintained by non-technical staff, requiring clear governance processes and simple update procedures.
informationArchitecture: The guide was organized into five sections: Voice & Tone, Writing Standards, Page Templates, Component Standards, and Governance & Process. Each section was designed to be usable as a standalone reference, with cross-links to related guidance. A quick-reference card was created for the most common content tasks.
userFlows: The guide addressed three primary contributor workflows: creating a new location page, writing a patient service description, and updating seasonal or time-sensitive content. Step-by-step process guides were developed for each workflow, integrated with the relevant standards sections.
wireframesAndPrototypes: Annotated page mockups were created showing correct application of content standards for each page template type. These served as both specification documents and training materials, illustrating the 'why' behind each standard.
requirementsAndCriteria: The guide included a content quality checklist covering plain language requirements, accessibility standards, brand voice criteria, and required metadata. Review and approval workflows were specified for content types with clinical or legal implications.
qaAndIteration: A pilot group of 5 content contributors tested the guide in a 2-week trial, creating new content using only the guide as reference. Feedback was incorporated in two revision cycles, primarily improving the clarity of the page template section and adding more before/after writing examples.
outcomesAndNextSteps: The guide was adopted organization-wide and reduced average content review cycles from 3 rounds to 1.5. Content contributors reported significantly higher confidence in publishing decisions. Next steps include annual review and update process, expansion to social media standards, and integration with the planned CMS replatforming project.

title: One Dog at a Time Colorado Audience Analysis & Content Strategy
strategicSummary: Conducted audience research and developed a content strategy to help a local animal rescue nonprofit better connect with adopters, volunteers, and donors.
responsibilities: Designed and administered audience surveys
Conducted interviews with adopters and volunteers
Analyzed existing web analytics and social media data
Developed audience personas and journey maps
Created content strategy recommendations
Prioritized content roadmap with the nonprofit team
overview: One Dog at a Time Colorado is a small volunteer-run rescue organization placing dogs from rural shelters into local foster and adoptive homes. Despite strong community support, their digital presence was not effectively converting interested visitors into adopters, fosters, or donors. This project used audience research to identify the gaps between what the organization communicated and what their audiences needed to take action.
problemAndGoals: Web analytics showed high traffic but low conversion on key actions: adoption applications, foster sign-ups, and donation completions. The organization needed to understand why interested visitors were not completing these actions and what content or structural changes would improve outcomes.
myRole: As the sole researcher and strategist on this project, I designed the research plan, administered all data collection, synthesized findings, and developed the content strategy recommendations. I worked directly with the organization's volunteer director to ensure recommendations were realistic for their capacity.
discoveryAndConstraints: Research included a 15-question survey distributed to the existing email list (n=87 responses), interviews with 6 recent adopters, 4 current fosters, and 3 lapsed donors, and review of 6 months of web analytics and social media performance data. The primary constraint was the organization's all-volunteer capacity—any recommendations needed to be implementable without paid staff.
informationArchitecture: Analysis revealed that visitors were arriving primarily to see available dogs, but the path from browsing dogs to understanding the adoption process was unclear. The recommended IA changes included surfacing the adoption process earlier in the user journey, creating a dedicated foster page with a clear FAQ, and restructuring the donation page around impact stories rather than organizational needs.
userFlows: Three revised user flows were designed: the potential adopter journey (from dog browsing through application submission), the potential foster journey (from curiosity through first placement), and the donor journey (from interest through recurring giving setup). Each flow identified specific content needs at each step.
wireframesAndPrototypes: Lightweight wireframes were created for the three highest-priority pages: the homepage, the adoption process page, and the foster information page. These were presented to the volunteer team with content recommendations, not as final designs.
requirementsAndCriteria: Content recommendations were prioritized using an impact/effort matrix, allowing the volunteer team to sequence implementation realistically. Each recommendation included a content brief specifying the goal, audience, key messages, and success criteria.
qaAndIteration: Recommendations were reviewed with the volunteer director and two board members, who validated the research findings from their own experience. One iteration cycle refined the foster page recommendations based on feedback about the organization's foster intake process.
outcomesAndNextSteps: The content strategy was delivered as a prioritized roadmap with 12 specific recommendations. The organization implemented the top 5 recommendations over 3 months and reported a measurable increase in foster applications. Next steps include a follow-up analytics review and expansion of the strategy to email and social media.

title: Furniture Flipping App Concept
strategicSummary: Designed UX strategy and information architecture for a mobile app concept connecting furniture flippers with local buyers, focusing on trust, transaction clarity, and community.
responsibilities: Conducted competitive analysis of resale platforms
Facilitated user interviews with sellers and buyers
Developed app concept and value proposition
Designed information architecture and navigation model
Created user flows for core transaction scenarios
Built interactive prototype in Figma
overview: Furniture flipping—buying, refinishing, and reselling used furniture—is a growing side economy with an active community of creators and buyers. Existing resale platforms were not designed for the unique needs of this niche: buyers want to see transformation stories, sellers need to communicate craft and quality, and transactions require local coordination. This concept project explored what a purpose-built platform for this community would look like.
problemAndGoals: Furniture flippers using general resale platforms reported frustration with low visibility for their work, difficulty communicating quality and provenance, and safety concerns around local meetups. The concept aimed to design an app that addressed these specific friction points while creating a community-centered transaction experience.
myRole: This was an independent concept project. I owned all phases from research through interactive prototype, treating it as a full UX strategy engagement to develop and demonstrate my process.
discoveryAndConstraints: Research included competitive analysis of 8 resale platforms (Facebook Marketplace, Craigslist, OfferUp, Chairish, and others), interviews with 5 active furniture flippers, and observation of online furniture flipping communities. The primary design constraint was mobile-first: the target audience managed all selling activity from their phones.
informationArchitecture: The app was organized around three core modes: Browse (discovery and shopping), Sell (listing creation and management), and Community (inspiration and connection). A persistent bottom navigation enabled quick switching between modes. Listing structure was designed to support transformation storytelling with before/after photos, materials documentation, and process notes.
userFlows: Primary flows designed: creating a listing with transformation story, discovering and purchasing a local item, scheduling a pickup meetup, and leaving a seller review. Safety features were integrated into the meetup flow, including location sharing and confirmation steps.
wireframesAndPrototypes: A complete interactive prototype was built in Figma covering the browse, listing, and transaction flows. The prototype included 40+ screens with realistic content and was tested with 4 participants from the furniture flipping community.
requirementsAndCriteria: A feature requirements document specified MVP scope versus future phases, covering listing fields, transaction flow requirements, community features, and trust and safety requirements. Accessibility requirements were included for the MVP, covering touch target sizing, color contrast, and screen reader support.
qaAndIteration: Prototype testing revealed that the listing creation flow was too long for mobile completion in a single session. The flow was redesigned to support saving drafts and resuming, and the step count was reduced from 7 to 4 by consolidating related fields. A second test round validated the revised flow.
outcomesAndNextSteps: The prototype was well-received in community feedback sessions, with participants specifically calling out the transformation story format and the safety-integrated meetup flow as differentiators. Next steps for the concept include a technical feasibility review, business model exploration, and a higher-fidelity prototype for investor presentation.
